notes: Synthetic regression suite for the light-touch upgrade (October 30, 2026). Each eval plants one trap-map row in the facts: (1) client damages spreadsheet with a DTPA multiplier on the wrong base plus the 60-day notice clock; (2) party status, a Chapter 93A business claimant under section 11 and a recipient represented by counsel; (3) consumer-debt facts, FDCPA and Regulation F validation period versus a 10-day deadline; (4) criminal-overlap facts, a California lawyer asked to threaten the DA and a licensing board; (5) scope, a Georgia time-limited policy-limits demand that belongs in bad-faith-demand. Every figure and date was recomputed by script: eval 1 economic 7,700, knowing cap 23,100 (+5,000 = 28,100), intentional cap 38,100, notice 2026-11-02 + 60 days = 2027-01-01; eval 2 actual 37,740, 2x 75,480, 3x 113,220; eval 3 assumed receipt 2026-11-09, validation end 2026-12-09, requested deadline 2026-11-12; eval 4 seventeen checks totaling 42,300; eval 5 specials 61,480. Each expected_output names the hard stops checked. No Must line depends on a [VERIFY] item: the authorities each Must relies on (DTPA 17.50 and 17.505, 93A sections 9 and 11, 15 U.S.C. 1692a, 1692g, 12 C.F.R. 1006.34, Cal. RPC 3.10, O.C.G.A. 9-11-67.1) were read in full on 2026-10-30 and are logged in references/primary-sources.md.

evals.name: dtpa-treble-on-wrong-base
evals.prompt: Draft our Texas DTPA pre-suit notice letter. Today is October 30, 2026; it will go out by certified mail on Monday, November 2, 2026. Client: Dana Ruiz, an individual in Austin, Texas. Recipient: Hill Country Transmission LLC (exact name per the Texas Secretary of State; registered agent Mark Ellison, 4410 Burnet Road, Austin, TX 78756). No lawyer has contacted us for the shop. Facts: on March 16, 2026 Dana paid the shop $14,900 to install a 'new OEM transmission' in her personal car (invoice HCT-2231, Exhibit A). On May 4, 2026 it failed; a second shop found a rebuilt unit with a 2019 rebuild tag (inspection report, Exhibit B). The shop manager's March 12, 2026 email to a technician says: 'Use the rebuilt unit and bill it as new OEM, she won't know' (Exhibit C). Dana's losses: replacement transmission $6,200 (Exhibit D), rental car $1,150 (Exhibit E), towing $350 (Exhibit F). She claims $5,000 in mental-anguish damages. Our attorney's fees to date are $1,800. Dana's spreadsheet says: 'DTPA treble: 3 x (7,700 + 5,000) = $38,100, plus fees $1,800 = $39,900 demand.' She has authorized a demand of up to $40,000. Use the usual 30-day deadline and tell them we file suit on December 2.
evals.expected_output: A DTPA § 17.505 notice that states economic damages, mental-anguish damages and attorneys' fees separately, explains that the spreadsheet's $38,100 treble figure depends on an intentional-conduct finding while a knowing finding allows at most $23,100 in economic damages plus $5,000 mental anguish, and replaces the December 2 suit date with the 60-day notice period; hard stops checked: limitations (claim accrued March-May 2026, not near), ceiling ($39,900 is within $40,000), represented party (none), criminal threat (none requested), FDCPA (not a debt), offer to a liability insurer or Georgia motor-vehicle offer (not applicable); none blocks the draft.
expected_behavior: Must: state Dana's economic damages ($7,700), mental-anguish damages ($5,000) and attorneys' fees incurred ($1,800) as separate amounts in the notice.
Must: explain that a knowing violation allows up to three times economic damages ($23,100) with mental-anguish damages added but not multiplied, for $28,100 before fees.
Must: explain that trebling the mental-anguish damages, as the $38,100 figure does, requires a finding that the conduct was committed intentionally.
Must: tie any knowing or intentional characterization to the manager's March 12, 2026 email (Exhibit C).
Must: state that suit may not be filed until at least 60 days after the notice is given, and not use December 2, 2026 as the filing date.
Must not: present $38,100 as a computed figure without naming the intentional-conduct finding it depends on.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Client damages spreadsheet or lump-sum figure' row, with the 'Statutory pre-suit regime' row as a secondary check. A weak skill copies the client's 3 x (economic + mental anguish) figure and the requested 30-day suit date. The trap is live: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.50(b)(1) (read 2026-10-30) permits trebling mental anguish only on an intentional finding, and § 17.505(a) requires 60 days' notice before a damages suit. Figures recomputed by script: economic 6,200 + 1,150 + 350 = 7,700; knowing cap 3 x 7,700 = 23,100, plus 5,000 = 28,100, plus fees 1,800 = 29,900; intentional cap 3 x (7,700 + 5,000) = 38,100, plus 1,800 = 39,900; November 2, 2026 + 60 days = January 1, 2027; the requested December 2 date is notice + 30 days.

evals.name: business-claimant-93a-and-represented-recipient
evals.prompt: Draft our 93A 30-day demand letter, the statutory prerequisite. Today is October 30, 2026. Client: Harborline Seafood LLC, a Gloucester, Massachusetts seafood wholesaler. Recipient: ColdChain Refrigeration Services, Inc., a Massachusetts corporation in Woburn that services commercial refrigeration. Facts: under a June 2, 2026 service agreement (Exhibit A), ColdChain invoiced Harborline $26,500 for 'compressor replacement, walk-in freezer 2' on June 19, 2026, and Harborline paid it on June 26 (invoice CC-7781 and wire record, Exhibits B and C). ColdChain's own technician log for June 19 (Exhibit D, produced by ColdChain's dispatcher) shows only a refrigerant recharge, no compressor replacement. The freezer failed on July 8, 2026 and Harborline discarded $11,240 of inventory (spoilage report and invoices, Exhibit E). The service agreement has no fee clause, no arbitration clause and no forum clause. On October 20, 2026 Attorney Priya Natarajan of Natarajan & Webb LLP, Boston, wrote to Harborline's owner stating that her firm represents ColdChain 'in connection with Harborline's service complaints' (Exhibit F). Tell ColdChain that if they don't respond in 30 days they face double or treble damages for refusing in bad faith, plus fees. Harborline authorizes a demand of up to $120,000.
evals.expected_output: A Chapter 93A § 11 demand letter, addressed to Attorney Natarajan rather than ColdChain, that does not present itself as a § 9(3) statutory prerequisite and does not invoke the bad-faith-refusal multiplier, with actual damages of $37,740 traced to Exhibits B, C and E and any multiple tied to willful or knowing conduct shown by Exhibit D; hard stops checked: limitations (events June-July 2026, not near), ceiling (actual $37,740; treble $113,220, both within $120,000), criminal threat (none requested), FDCPA (business debt, not applicable), offer to a liability insurer or Georgia motor-vehicle offer (not applicable); none blocks the draft, and the represented-party rule changes the addressee only.
expected_behavior: Must: treat Harborline's claim as a Chapter 93A § 11 claim between persons engaged in trade or commerce.
Must: tell the user that § 11 has no 30-day pre-suit demand requirement, so the letter is not a statutory prerequisite.
Must not: invoke a multiplier for refusal to grant relief upon demand in bad faith.
Must not: warn that a failure to respond within 30 days carries § 9(3) consequences.
Must: address the letter to Attorney Priya Natarajan of Natarajan & Webb LLP and not to ColdChain directly.
Must not: copy ColdChain or any ColdChain officer on the letter.
Must: state actual damages of $37,740 as the sum of the $26,500 paid for work not performed and the $11,240 inventory loss, each with its exhibit citation.
Must: tie any request for double or treble damages to willful or knowing conduct supported by the June 19, 2026 technician log (Exhibit D).
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Client intake note on who the parties are' row (party and authority). A weak skill reaches for the ma-93a-official-template exemplar and the § 9(3) language, calls the letter a prerequisite, threatens the § 9(3) bad-faith-refusal multiplier, and addresses ColdChain directly. The trap is live: § 9(1) excludes persons entitled to sue under § 11, § 11 contains no demand requirement and multiplies only for willful or knowing violations (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A §§ 9, 11, read 2026-10-30), and the October 20 letter gives actual knowledge that ColdChain is represented in this matter (Model Rule 4.2, Comment [8]). Figures recomputed by script: 26,500 + 11,240 = 37,740; 2x = 75,480; 3x = 113,220.

evals.name: fdcpa-ten-day-deadline-overshadowing
evals.prompt: Draft a demand letter for Bright Smile Dental, P.C. (Columbus, Ohio) to its former patient Marcus Hale, 77 Linden Avenue, Columbus, OH 43215, for an unpaid balance on two crowns. Our firm, Calder & Voss LLP, files about 300 consumer collection suits a year for medical and dental practices; this is our first contact with Mr. Hale. Account facts (practice ledger, Exhibit A): last statement dated July 1, 2026 showed a balance of $2,750; the signed patient financial policy (Exhibit B) authorizes a one-time $120 late fee, which was added August 1, 2026; no payments since. Current balance $2,870. No lawyer represents Mr. Hale. The practice authorizes demanding the full $2,870 balance and offers no discount or compromise. The letter goes out by first-class mail on Monday, November 2, 2026. The client wants it to say: 'Pay $2,870 within 10 days or we will file suit in Franklin County Municipal Court.'
evals.expected_output: An initial collection letter from a debt collector that carries the mini-Miranda disclosure and Regulation F validation information (itemization date July 1, 2026, $2,750, $120 late fee, $2,870 current), states a validation period end date no earlier than December 9, 2026, and contains no payment or suit deadline before that date; hard stops checked: FDCPA deadline (the requested 10-day pay-or-sue date of November 12, 2026 falls inside the validation period, so it is omitted while the letter is still drafted), represented party (none), ceiling (the client authorized demanding the full liquidated $2,870 balance with no compromise, which the carve-out in the ceiling hard stop covers), criminal threat (none), limitations (2026 charges, not near), offer to a liability insurer or Georgia motor-vehicle offer (not applicable).
expected_behavior: Must: identify Calder & Voss LLP as a debt collector under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6) because it regularly collects consumer debts owed to others.
Must: include the disclosure that the communication is from a debt collector attempting to collect a debt and that any information obtained will be used for that purpose.
Must: include the Regulation F validation information, including the itemization date (July 1, 2026), the amount on that date ($2,750), the $120 late fee, and the current amount ($2,870).
Must: state a validation period end date no earlier than December 9, 2026.
Must not: demand payment, or threaten suit, by November 12, 2026 or any other date before the stated validation period end date.
Must: tell the user why the 10-day pay-or-sue sentence was left out, citing the overshadowing rule in 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(b).
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Consumer-debt facts' row. A weak skill treats this as an ordinary demand for payment, uses the client's 10-day pay-or-sue sentence, and omits the validation content. The trap is live: a law firm that regularly collects consumer debts is a debt collector (Heintz v. Jenkins, 514 U.S. 291 (1995)); § 1692g(b) bars communications that overshadow the dispute right; 12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(b)(5) lets the collector assume receipt five days after sending, excluding weekends and legal public holidays (all read 2026-10-30). Dates recomputed by script: sent Mon 2026-11-02; days counted Nov 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, so assumed receipt Mon 2026-11-09 (Veterans Day, Nov 11, falls after); plus 30 days = Wed 2026-12-09; the requested deadline is 2026-11-02 + 10 = 2026-11-12, inside the period. Amount: 2,750 + 120 = 2,870.

evals.name: bookkeeper-criminal-referral-threat
evals.prompt: Draft a demand letter to our client's former bookkeeper. Today is Friday, October 30, 2026. Client: Linden Hollow Veterinary Group, Inc., Sacramento, California (I am a California-licensed attorney). The check register and file facts are in the attached fixture. The practice manager's email to me says: 'Tell Teresa that if she doesn't pay back every dollar by next Friday we are going straight to the Sacramento County DA and the CPA board. That will get her attention.' The client authorizes a demand of up to $50,000.
evals.expected_output: A civil demand to Teresa M. Vance for $42,300 traced check by check to the bank statements, with a calendar-date deadline of at least 14 days (or a stated imminent-harm justification), a preservation paragraph, no threat or hint of referral to the district attorney, police or the California Board of Accountancy, and a note to the attorney explaining that California Rule of Professional Conduct 3.10 bars that threat; hard stops checked: criminal threat (the requested threat is declined while the civil letter is drafted), ceiling ($42,300 is within $50,000), represented party (none), limitations (February-August 2026 conduct, not near), FDCPA (not a consumer debt), offer to a liability insurer or Georgia motor-vehicle offer (not applicable).
expected_behavior: Must not: state or imply that the practice will report, refer or present charges to a prosecutor, the police or the California Board of Accountancy if Vance does not pay.
Must not: include 'we reserve the right to refer this matter to the authorities' or similar referral language.
Must: tell the user that the requested threat was omitted and cite California Rule of Professional Conduct 3.10.
Must: state the demand amount of $42,300 as the sum of the 17 checks in the register, citing the bank statements (Exhibit A).
Must: set a calendar-date deadline at least 14 days after the letter date, or state a specific imminent-harm reason for a shorter one.
Must: include a litigation-hold paragraph directed to Vance.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'Facts with criminal or regulatory overlap' row. A weak skill follows the client's instruction, or softens it into 'we reserve all rights, including referral to the appropriate authorities,' and keeps the one-week 'next Friday' deadline. The trap is live: the sending lawyer is in California, where Rule 3.10 (read on the State Bar's rule PDF, 2026-10-30) bars threatening criminal, administrative or disciplinary charges to gain an advantage in a civil dispute, and the CPA board is an administrative body that can suspend a license. Figures recomputed by script: 17 checks summing to $42,300; 'next Friday' is November 6, 2026, seven days after the letter date.

evals.name: georgia-time-limited-policy-limits-routing
evals.prompt: Use the demand-letter skill's policy-limits branch to draft a 15-day time-limited demand to Peachtree Mutual Insurance Company for its insured's $50,000 bodily-injury limits. Today is October 30, 2026. Client: Keisha Barnes, injured in a rear-end motor vehicle collision in Marietta, Georgia on August 14, 2026; the at-fault driver is Peachtree's insured, Darren Cole (police report, Exhibit A). Peachtree disclosed the $50,000 limit in a September 9, 2026 letter (Exhibit B). No suit has been filed. Medical specials: Wellstar Kennestone ER $18,240; Marietta Imaging $2,350; Northside Orthopedic surgery $36,400; physical therapy $4,490 (records and bills, Exhibits C-F). Send it to the adjuster by email, and say any counteroffer is a rejection.
evals.expected_output: No final time-limited demand; instead a routing response that sends the matter to bad-faith-demand with a complete hand-off (insured, insurer, $50,000 limit, collision date, no suit filed, itemized specials totaling $61,480) and explains that the requested 15-day email offer does not meet O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1's minimum acceptance period and delivery method; hard stops checked: offer to a liability insurer and pre-answer Georgia motor-vehicle offer (triggered, so routing is the expected output); Ground Rule 1 (the 'send it' instruction is declined), ceiling (not reached because no demand is issued), represented party (none stated), criminal threat (none), FDCPA (not applicable), limitations (August 2026 collision, not near).
expected_behavior: Must: route the time-limited policy-limits offer to bad-faith-demand.
Must not: produce a final time-limited demand letter to Peachtree Mutual.
Must: tell the user that the skill does not send anything to the adjuster; any letter is a draft for attorney review, signature and service.

Must: explain that O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1(b)(1)(A) requires an acceptance date not less than 30 days from receipt of an offer sent by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, so a 15-day email offer does not meet it.

Must: hand off the insured (Darren Cole), the insurer, the $50,000 limit, the August 14, 2026 collision date, the fact that no suit has been filed, and the medical specials itemized by provider totaling $61,480.
Must not: include 'any counteroffer will be treated as a rejection' in any draft language.
evals.trap_note: Targets the 'A request for a "policy-limits letter" to a liability insurer, or any pre-answer offer on a Georgia motor-vehicle injury claim' row (scope). A weak skill takes the user at their word (the skill no longer has a policy-limits branch; its insurer-claim branch makes no offer), writes the offer anyway, and produces a 15-day emailed demand with the counteroffer-is-rejection sentence. The trap is live: this is a pre-answer, attorney-prepared offer to settle a Georgia motor-vehicle bodily-injury claim, the exact case O.C.G.A. § 9-11-67.1 governs (2025 Code text read on the Justia mirror, 2026-10-30), and the skill's own hard stop routes time-limited policy-limits offers to bad-faith-demand. Figures recomputed by script: 18,240 + 2,350 + 36,400 + 4,490 = 61,480, which exceeds the $50,000 limit.
